difficultyReason: The stimulus blends quantitative data with a qualifying exception (urban versus rural patients). The correct answer respects both the general trend and the exception. Traps include one too-strong answer that drops the qualifier, one that inverts the direction, and one plausible-but-unsupported claim about treatment access.
stimulus: A county health department reviewed hospital admission records for patients diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes over a five-year period. Among patients living in urban areas, roughly 60 percent had received a formal nutritional counseling session within the twelve months preceding diagnosis. Among patients living in rural areas, fewer than 20 percent had received such counseling in the same window. Across both groups, patients who had received counseling were, on average, diagnosed at an earlier stage of the disease than those who had not. The department also noted that rural hospitals in the county had, on average, half as many registered dietitians on staff per one hundred beds as urban hospitals.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nutritional counseling prevents the onset of Type 2 diabetes in patients who would otherwise develop the condition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rural patients in the county had less access to nutritional counseling services than urban patients did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing the number of dietitians at rural hospitals would eliminate the disparity in diabetes outcomes between rural and urban patients.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban patients who did not receive nutritional counseling were diagnosed at a later stage of diabetes than rural patients who did receive it.
choices.text2: Urban patients who did not receive nutritional counseling were diagnosed at a later stage of diabetes than rural patients who did receive it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Among patients in the county, receiving nutritional counseling is the most important factor in achieving an early diabetes diagnosis.

explanations.correct: The stimulus states that fewer than 20% of rural patients received counseling versus roughly 60% of urban patients, and that rural hospitals have half as many dietitians per bed. Together these facts strongly support the claim that rural patients had less access to such services — a hedged, comparative inference grounded directly in the data.
explanations.A: Too strong and out-of-scope: the stimulus shows a correlation between counseling and earlier-stage diagnosis, not that counseling prevents onset. This commits the opposite-direction trap by implying prevention rather than detection timing.
explanations.B: Correct. Both the lower counseling rate and the lower dietitian staffing ratio in rural areas directly support this comparative, hedged claim.
explanations.C: Too strong: the stimulus provides no basis for concluding that adding dietitians would 'eliminate' the disparity. This is a scope-creep and absolute-language trap.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus gives group-level averages for counseled versus non-counseled patients across both groups combined; it does not provide a cross-group comparison of urban non-counseled patients versus rural counseled patients.
explanations.E: Too strong: 'most important factor' introduces a ranking that the stimulus never establishes. This is an extreme-language trap.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents economic data with a controlled twist: a general trend (rising automation correlates with lower wages for low-skill work) coexists with an exception (one sector where automation correlates with higher wages). The correct answer draws a hedged inference from the exception. Traps include an inversion of the general trend, an absolute overclaim, and a plausible-but-unstated policy conclusion.
stimulus: An analysis of manufacturing employment data from thirty-two countries between 2005 and 2020 found that in twenty-six of those countries, the introduction of automated assembly systems correlated with a decline in average hourly wages for workers classified as low-skill. In five countries, no statistically significant wage change was observed. In one country — a small economy with a highly specialized electronics sector — automation correlated with a substantial increase in average hourly wages for low-skill workers, a pattern researchers attributed to a concurrent sharp reduction in the available labor pool caused by demographic contraction.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In most of the countries studied, the introduction of automated assembly systems was associated with lower average hourly wages for low-skill manufacturing workers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Automation of manufacturing processes invariably reduces wages for low-skill workers unless the labor supply simultaneously contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Countries that introduce automated assembly systems should expect low-skill wages to decline within five years.
choices.text2: Countries that introduce automated assembly systems should expect low-skill wages to decline within five years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The negative effect of automation on low-skill wages is stronger in large economies than in small, specialized ones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Demographic contraction is the primary driver of wage growth in low-skill manufacturing sectors across the countries studied.

explanations.correct: Twenty-six of thirty-two countries showed a correlation between automation and declining low-skill wages. 'Most' accurately captures 26/32 (over 80%), and 'associated with' is appropriately hedged — no causal claim is made. This is a direct, proportional inference from the data.
explanations.A: Correct. 26 out of 32 countries clearly constitutes 'most,' and the language mirrors the correlational framing of the stimulus.
explanations.B: Too strong: 'invariably' is an absolute claim. The stimulus shows five countries with no significant change, meaning wage decline is not invariable even setting aside the exceptional case. This is an extreme-language trap.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus provides historical correlations but does not support a forward-looking prescriptive prediction with a specific timeline. This is a scope-creep trap.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus describes only one small-economy outlier and attributes the anomaly to labor-pool contraction, not to size per se. No systematic comparison by economy size is offered.
explanations.E: Too strong and mis-scoped: the stimulus mentions demographic contraction only in connection with one country's exceptional outcome; it says nothing about demographic contraction as a driver across the broader sample.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents linguistic fieldwork data with a qualification about language contact. The correct answer draws a modest inference about a subgroup. Traps include one too-strong universal claim, one inversion, one that introduces unsupported causal direction, and one plausible-but-unstated generalization about language endangerment.
stimulus: Fieldwork conducted among speakers of seventeen endangered languages in the Pacific region documented the phonological features of each language as spoken by its oldest surviving fluent speakers (those aged 65 and above) and by its youngest fluent speakers (those aged 18 to 30). In eleven of the seventeen languages, the youngest speakers used a reduced consonant inventory compared with the oldest speakers — a pattern the researchers attributed to prolonged contact with a regional trade language that itself has a relatively sparse consonant inventory. In the six remaining languages, no significant difference in consonant inventory was observed between age groups, and none of those six languages had experienced sustained contact with the trade language.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contact with a language that has a sparse consonant inventory will eventually cause any endangered language to lose consonant distinctions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among the endangered languages studied, those that had sustained contact with the regional trade language were more likely to show a reduction in consonant inventory across generations than those that had not.
choices.text2: Among the endangered languages studied, those that had sustained contact with the regional trade language were more likely to show a reduction in consonant inventory across generations than those that had not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Younger speakers of endangered languages are generally less proficient in those languages than older speakers are.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The regional trade language expanded its consonant inventory as a result of contact with the endangered languages in the study.
choices.text2: The regional trade language expanded its consonant inventory as a result of contact with the endangered languages in the study.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A language's consonant inventory is the phonological feature most susceptible to change under conditions of language contact.

explanations.correct: All eleven languages that showed consonant reduction had trade-language contact; none of the six languages without such contact showed reduction. This perfectly aligns the contact condition with the outcome, strongly supporting a comparative claim about likelihood within the study sample. The answer is appropriately scoped to 'the endangered languages studied' and uses hedged comparative language ('more likely').
explanations.A: Too strong: 'will eventually cause any endangered language' is a universal, predictive absolute. The stimulus shows a correlation in a specific sample and cannot sustain that sweeping claim. This is an extreme-language trap.
explanations.B: Correct. The data show 11/11 contact languages with reduction and 0/6 non-contact languages with reduction, directly supporting this hedged comparative inference scoped to the study.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus documents differences in consonant inventory, not overall proficiency levels. This introduces a concept — proficiency — absent from the stimulus, making it a plausible-but-unsupported trap.
explanations.D: Opposite direction: the stimulus describes influence flowing from the trade language to the endangered languages (reduced consonant inventory in the latter), not the reverse. This is a classic inversion trap.
explanations.E: Too strong and unsupported: the stimulus examines only consonant inventory and offers no comparison to other phonological features. Claiming it is the 'most susceptible' feature goes far beyond what the data establish. This is an absolute-ranking trap.
